extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology, literary studies, and narrative theory
extracted.subtask_description: Principled criteria and concepts for analyzing and describing narrative texts (text, story, fabula), narrator and focalization, and the processes that order fabular elements into stories, aimed at guiding literary/narratological analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text as finite structured whole composed of signs
rubrics_metrics.description: A text is a finite, structured whole composed of signs. These can be linguistic units, such as words and sentences, but they can also be different signs, such as cinematic shots and sequences, or painted dots, lines, and blots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The finiteness refers to identifiable first and last elements (first/last word, image, frame) though such boundaries are provisional and porous. The concept of 'text' is used with emphasis on finiteness and structured nature, not only linguistic form. Example: comic strips are narrative texts if the notion of text is interpreted broadly to include visual sign systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a narrative text
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative text is a text in which an agent or subject conveys to an addressee ('tells' the reader, viewer, or listener) a story in a medium, such as language, imagery, sound, buildings, or a combination thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between 'text' (the physical/material signs), 'story' (the way elements are presented), and 'fabula' (the series of events in the imagined world). The story is the content that produces a particular manifestation of a fabula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabula (series of events) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A fabula is a series of logically and chronologically related events that are caused or experienced by actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fabula elements include events, actors, time, and location. Events are transitions from one state to another; actors are agents who perform actions (not necessarily human). The fabula is the material/content that is worked into a story; its meanings and effects are not limited by the finite text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabula elements: events, actors, time, location
rubrics_metrics.description: A fabula's material consists of events, actors, time, and location — events always take up time and occur somewhere; actors cause or experience events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elements are the raw material of fabula and must be attended to in analysis (e.g., Tom Thumb's seven-mile boots affecting the timing of escape). Analysts should consider how each element functions in the fabula and how its manipulation in the story produces effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-layer distinction: text, story, fabula
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative analysis rests on a three-part division: text (material signs), story (ordering and presentation of fabula elements), and fabula (chronological/logical events in the imagined world).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These layers can be described separately for analytic clarity even though they are intertwined in practice. Text is the only materially accessible layer; story is an arranged version of fabula; fabula is a mental reconstruction by the reader. This theoretical disjunction is instrumental and provisional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering processes that produce a story — sequence vs chronology
rubrics_metrics.description: Events in the fabula are arranged in a sequence in the story that can differ from the chronological sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should note deviations between fabular chronology and the story's presentation (e.g., flashbacks, anachronies) and evaluate their effects on meaning and reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering processes that produce a story — allocation of narrative time
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of time allotted in the story to the various elements of the fabula is determined with respect to the amount of time these elements take up in the fabula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider narrative duration, ellipses, expansion, and contraction; how much narrative attention is given versus how much fabular time elapses, and what effects this produces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering processes that produce a story — character individuation
rubrics_metrics.description: The actors are provided with distinct traits; thus they are individualized and transformed into characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze characterization techniques (traits, behaviour, speech) and how they make actors into narrative characters who drive interpretation and affective responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering processes that produce a story — place transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: The locations where events occur are also given distinct characteristics and are thereby transformed into specific places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to how settings are described and shaped to become meaningful narrative places (e.g., symbolic or functional roles played by locations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering processes that produce a story — symbolic/allusive/traditional relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Other relationships — symbolic, allusive, traditional — may exist among the various elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for inter-element relations such as symbolism, allusion, intertextual traditions that structure meaning beyond linear events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering processes that produce a story — point of view and focalization
rubrics_metrics.description: A choice is made from among the various points of view from which the elements can be presented. The resulting focalization—the relation between who perceives and what is perceived—colours the story with subjectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the focalizer(s), the level(s) of focalization, and how point of view shapes interpretation and affects trust, sympathy, and narrative colouring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between text, story, and fabula as analytic tool
rubrics_metrics.description: The text is not identical to the story; the story is not identical to the fabula. The only material we have is the text; the story and fabula are theoretical constructions used for analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts must construct story and fabula from the text; recognize that fabula is a reader's interpretation influenced by story manipulations. Use the separations as provisional tools to make analyses explicit and discussable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator defined as textual agent distinct from author
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative agent or narrator is the (linguistic, visual, cinematic) subject — a function, not a person — which expresses itself in the language or images that constitute the text; this agent is not the biographical author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain distinction between narrator (function within the text) and author (historical person). The narrator can be referred to as 'it' to emphasize functional status. This distinction is crucial for narratological readings that avoid authorial-biographical fallacies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator and focalization jointly determine narrative situation
rubrics_metrics.description: The identity of the narrator, degree/manner it is indicated, and choices implied lend the text its specific character; narrator and focalization together determine the narrative situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between the narrating agent (who utters signs) and the focalizer (agent of perception). Analyze overlaps and separations among narrator, focalizer, and actor to understand narrative perspective and rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of narration: external vs character-bound narrator (I and He are both I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grammatically the narrating subject is always a 'first person' (a speaking subject). An external narrator does not figure as an actor in the fabula; a character-bound narrator identifies with a character who is an actor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize rhetorical consequences: character-bound narrators often imply autobiographical veracity; external narrators can adopt testimonial rhetoric. Examples and paraphrases (CN, EN) help shorthand notation of relationships among agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signalling fictionality and rhetoric of veracity
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative form and signals (e.g., 'Once upon a time', subtitles 'A Novel') can indicate fictionality; character-bound narration usually proclaims or implies truthful/autobiographical rhetoric, while other signals may indicate invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to rhetorical markers that establish claims to truth or fiction and evaluate how they affect reader belief and interpretive strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptible vs non-perceptible narrators and partial coincidence of agents
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator may manifest itself as an 'I' yet not be a character (non-perceptible as an actor), producing cases of partial coincidence among narrator, focalizer, and actor (e.g., EN(np) [EF [cF (Ott.)]-Steyn(p)] notation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use layered notation to map coincidences and non-coincidences of narrating, focalizing, and acting agents; this clarifies levels of subjectivity, partiality, and rhetorical stance in complex texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator as witness
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator can adopt the stance of a witness: remaining invisible yet committed to the story it tells, conveying compassion, irony, or other affective responses and influencing veracity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider ethical implications (modesty vs voyeurism), the witness's role in soliciting reader compassion, and how witness stance affects credibility and reader alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic practice: selectivity and compatibility with reception approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: The analyst will always make choices; intuition brings together striking aspects of an artefact and relevant theoretical elements. On the basis of careful reading and attention to reader response, select theory elements particularly relevant to the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theory is an instrument to make descriptions and interpretations arguable; interpretation must be grounded in precise description. The approach is compatible with reception-oriented methods because it acknowledges the role of reader response and intuition in selecting analytic foci.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative theory as cultural analysis and focus on agency/subjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative is a cultural phenomenon; narrativity and narratological concepts are influenced by cultural constraints and subjectivity. The theory emphasizes agency: narrators, focalizers, and actors as agents of perception and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation should consider cultural framing and how subjectivity arises at the intersection of individual and social existence. Use narrative analysis to study cultural processes and conditions of possibility for narrative practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of provisional definitions and explicitness
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions are provisional and serve to be explicit and transparent so that analysts know what is relevant for discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt working definitions to delimit analytic relevancies, while acknowledging their provisional nature; clarity of terms makes interpretation discussable rather than 'objective proof.'
